name: Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
summary: Mood stabilizer best known for preventing bipolar depression. It’s not a fast “calm down” med—this one is slow-build by design because rushing the dose can trigger dangerous rashes.
description: Lamotrigine is a long-game medication for bipolar disorder—especially the depression side. The tradeoff is titration: you start low and increase slowly to reduce the risk of serious skin reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS). If you get a new rash during the first 2–8 weeks, treat it like an emergency until proven otherwise and call your prescriber right away. It’s not effective for acute mania, and it’s not a PRN medication.
patient_summary: Lamotrigine is a long-game medication for bipolar disorder—especially the depression side. You don’t feel it in an hour. You build it over weeks. The slow titration isn’t optional: rushing can trigger dangerous rashes. New rash early on? Don’t “wait it out”—call your prescriber immediately. It’s not for acute mania and not a PRN.

primary_indications: Bipolar Depression (Acute episodes: commonly used; not for acute mania)

linked_conditions.context: FDA-labeled for maintenance treatment to delay mood episodes. Clinically, it’s often chosen when depression is the bigger problem than mania.
Often used for bipolar major depression as an alternative option, but it’s not a rapid antidepressant and it’s not effective for acute mania or hypomania.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to lamotrigine or any component of the formulation (eg, rash, angioedema, urticaria, mucosal ulceration)

efficacy_response.patient_text: Lamotrigine’s strength is maintenance—staying well over time, especially reducing the odds of sliding back into bipolar depression. It is not a fast-acting medication for acute mania.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed by mouth; food does not meaningfully change absorption
pharmacokinetics.onset: Not rapid; benefits typically emerge over weeks due to required slow titration
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate-release: ~1 to 5 hours; extended-release: ~4 to 11 hours (varies with interacting meds)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: ~25 to 33 hours (longer with valproate; shorter with enzyme inducers)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Typically dosed once or twice daily depending on dose and formulation
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily glucuronidation; major interactions with inhibitors (valproate) and inducers (carbamazepine/phenytoin/phenobarbital/primidone; rifampin)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food has no major effect on absorption

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Lamotrigine is a mood stabilizer used in {link:condition:bipolar-i-disorder:bipolar disorder}—especially when bipolar depression is the recurring issue. It’s a maintenance medication, meaning the goal is fewer episodes over time. It is not a good fit for acute mania because it ramps too slowly.
items: {link:condition:bipolar-i-disorder:Bipolar I disorder (maintenance)}: Helps delay future mood episodes over time
{link:condition:bipolar-depression:Bipolar depression}: Commonly used to target the depression side (slow-build, not an emergency fix)
off_label: Acute bipolar major depression (commonly used as an alternative option; titration limits speed)
Mood stabilization when antidepressants repeatedly trigger mood swings (situational; clinician-dependent)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Lamotrigine is not the kind of med you “feel” right away. Most people describe it as subtle—until they look back and realize things got steadier.

quotes: This wasn’t a ‘take it and feel better tonight’ thing. It was more like… week by week, my mood stopped free-falling.
At first I thought it wasn’t doing anything—then I noticed I wasn’t spiraling as hard.
My lows didn’t hit as deep or last as long.
I still had emotions—I just wasn’t getting trapped in them for weeks.
A little dizzy at first, like my brain was buffering.
Nausea for a few days, then it chilled out.
Sleep got weird for a bit—more vivid dreams.
items.note: Early side effects often fade as your body adjusts, but a new rash is different—don’t ignore it.

items.category: Rash anxiety (because the warning is real)
quotes: I got paranoid about every itchy spot, but honestly I’d rather be cautious than sorry.
My doctor drilled it into me: new rash early on = call immediately.
The starter pack made it easier to follow the schedule without messing up.
items.note: Most rashes are benign, but you can’t reliably predict which ones turn serious—so prescribers treat early rashes seriously.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Lamotrigine is intentionally slow because the main serious risk (dangerous rash) is strongly linked to starting too high or titrating too fast. So the timeline is measured in weeks, not hours.
key_points: Week 1–2: Usually a low starter dose (this is safety-focused, not symptom-focused)
Week 3–6: Gradual increases toward a therapeutic dose (most people start noticing changes during this window, if at all)
Maintenance: Benefits are typically about fewer relapses over time—especially fewer depressive episodes
Highest rash-risk window: Most life-threatening rashes occur within 2–8 weeks after starting (rare cases later can occur)
Half-life: Roughly 1 day in many adults, but it can be much longer with valproate and shorter with enzyme-inducing meds

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Lamotrigine is best thought of as a mood-stability and relapse-prevention medication—particularly for bipolar depression. It is not effective for acute mania or hypomania, and it’s not designed to be a rapid “rescue” medication.
sections.clinical_details: In clinical practice, lamotrigine is often chosen when a person’s bipolar pattern is depression-heavy, or when preventing depressive relapses is the priority. The slow titration is a built-in limitation for urgent symptom relief, so clinicians typically use other tools if someone is acutely manic or severely agitated.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: New rash early on is a big deal. Call your prescriber immediately—don’t self-triage this.
sections.black_box: Lamotrigine can cause serious rashes that require hospitalization and stopping the medication, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Risk increases with high starting doses, rapid titration, and use with valproate. Most life-threatening rashes occur within 2–8 weeks after starting, but rare late cases have been reported. Lamotrigine is usually stopped at the first sign of rash unless the rash is clearly not medication-related.
other: Do not exceed recommended starting doses or titration schedules—this is one of the clearest ways to reduce serious rash risk
Higher rash risk with valproate (valproic acid/divalproex) because it raises lamotrigine levels
Genetic risk: HLA-B*15:02 is linked to increased SJS/TEN risk in some populations (screening may be recommended based on ancestry and clinical context)
Multiorgan hypersensitivity reactions can occur (DRESS, blood dyscrasias, organ involvement). Fever + rash + swollen nodes = urgent evaluation
Rare immune syndrome: hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) can present with fever, rash, organ dysfunction, and blood count changes
Rare aseptic meningitis: headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia—especially if paired with rash or systemic symptoms
Suicidal thoughts/behavior warning applies to antiseizure medications as a class—monitor mood changes closely
Cardiac caution in people with structural/functional heart disease or conduction disorders (including Brugada pattern risk); extra monitoring may be needed in higher-risk patients
patient_counseling: Follow the titration schedule exactly. This is not a ‘take extra to catch up’ medication.

If you notice a new rash—especially in the first 2–8 weeks—contact your prescriber right away. If you have blisters, mouth sores, eye irritation, facial swelling, fever, or feel very sick: treat it as urgent.
If you stop lamotrigine for about a week or more, do not restart at your old dose. Restarting usually means starting low again.
Tell your clinician if you take valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, rifampin, or hormonal birth control—these can change lamotrigine levels a lot.
Monitor for new or worsening depression, agitation, or suicidal thoughts—especially early in treatment or after dose changes.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most people tolerate lamotrigine well, but the headline risk is rash. Common day-to-day side effects include dizziness, nausea, sleep changes, and headache-like symptoms.
plain_language_list: Fatigue or drowsiness (less common than many mood meds, but it happens)
Rash (most are mild; rare cases are severe and dangerous)

common.patient_note: Often shows up during dose increases. Standing up slowly, hydration, and avoiding alcohol/other sedatives can help. If dizziness is severe or persistent, the dose may be moving too fast.

common.incidence: Common (label reports nausea in a notable minority of adults)
common.patient_note: Taking with food can help. Many people find it fades after the first couple of weeks.
Some people feel more alert or have vivid dreams. Timing the dose earlier in the day can help for some, but dosing decisions should match your formulation and plan.
Not everyone gets this, but if you feel activated, irritable, or emotionally edgy after increases, tell your prescriber—sometimes slowing the titration fixes it.

common.incidence: Reported; serious rash is rare but high-stakes
common.patient_note: Any new rash early on should be treated seriously until proven otherwise. Do not try to self-diagnose this.

serious: Serious skin reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and rash-related hospitalization or death (rare but real).
DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms): rash plus fever, lymph node swelling, and possible organ involvement.
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH): persistent fever, rash, organ dysfunction, and blood count abnormalities.
Aseptic meningitis: headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia; can recur rapidly on re-exposure.
Blood dyscrasias: neutropenia, pancytopenia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia (rare).
Cardiac conduction issues/proarrhythmia risk in susceptible patients (especially with underlying conduction disease or other sodium channel blockers).
Suicidal thoughts or behavior (class warning for antiseizure medications).

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Lamotrigine interactions can be big enough to change the entire titration schedule. The two biggest categories are: (1) valproate, which raises lamotrigine levels, and (2) enzyme inducers, which lower levels. Hormonal estrogen can also lower levels and create swings across the pill cycle.

items.risk: Raises lamotrigine exposure and increases serious rash risk when dosing is not adjusted.
items.action: Use a lower starting dose and slower titration schedule. Never copy a ‘standard’ titration if valproate is on board.

items.with: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone) and other inducers (eg, rifampin)
items.risk: Lowers lamotrigine levels, which can reduce effectiveness and complicate switching between IR and XR.
items.action: Higher dosing targets and different titration schedules may be needed. If an inducer is stopped, lamotrigine levels can rise—dose adjustments should be planned, not reactive.

items.with: Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives (and other estrogen derivatives)
items.risk: Can lower lamotrigine levels by up to about half; during the pill-free interval, levels can rise—sometimes dramatically—creating a ‘roller coaster’ of side effects and symptom control.
items.action: Plan contraception and lamotrigine dosing together. Consider extended-cycle options and therapeutic drug monitoring when starting/stopping estrogen-containing contraception.

items.with: Other sodium channel blockers or conduction-impairing substances
items.risk: May increase proarrhythmic risk in susceptible patients.
items.action: Use extra caution in patients with known cardiac disease or conduction disorders; consider ECG monitoring strategies when indicated.

items.risk: Can worsen dizziness, sedation, and coordination issues.
items.action: If you drink, keep it minimal and consistent and avoid combining with dose increases; safest option is to avoid alcohol during titration.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Lamotrigine should not be stopped abruptly unless there’s a serious safety concern (like a suspected severe rash). For routine discontinuation, tapering lowers the risk of withdrawal symptoms and helps prevent mood destabilization.
key_points: Typical taper approach: Reduce the dose by about 50% per week and taper over at least 2 weeks (longer tapers are often used in practice based on history and stability).
Bipolar context: After stopping, monitor for weeks to months for recurrence of depression, hypomania, or mania.
If lamotrigine is stopped due to rash: Do not restart unless a specialist explicitly determines it is safe (often it is avoided).
If treatment is interrupted for about a week or more (roughly ≥5 half-lives): Restart using the initial titration schedule rather than jumping back to the prior dose.
If you are changing interacting meds (starting/stopping valproate, enzyme inducers, or estrogen): plan dose adjustments gradually to avoid sudden spikes or drops in lamotrigine levels.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Lamotrigine dosing is all about the titration schedule. The starting dose and weekly increases change depending on interacting medications—especially valproate (lower/slow) and enzyme inducers (higher/faster).

adult.bipolar_no_interacting_meds_titration: Weeks 3–4: 50 mg/day; Week 5: 100 mg/day; Week 6: 200 mg/day (in 1–2 doses depending on formulation)
adult.bipolar_no_interacting_meds_target: 200 mg/day is the labeled maintenance target for many adults; some patients may require up to 400 mg/day based on response and tolerability
adult.bipolar_with_valproate_initial: Weeks 1–2: 25 mg PO every other day
adult.bipolar_with_valproate_titration: Weeks 3–4: 25 mg PO once daily; Week 5: 50 mg/day; Week 6 and maintenance: 100 mg/day (in 1–2 doses depending on formulation)
adult.bipolar_with_inducers_initial: Weeks 1–2: 50 mg/day (in 1–2 doses depending on formulation)
adult.bipolar_with_inducers_titration: Weeks 3–4: 100 mg/day; Week 5: 200 mg/day; Week 6: 300 mg/day; Maintenance: up to 400 mg/day (in 1–2 doses depending on formulation)
adult.er_dosing: Extended-release (XR) is dosed once daily; immediate-release is once daily when total daily dose is ≤25 mg and typically twice daily when >25 mg
adult.restart_after_interruption: If lamotrigine has been stopped for ≥6 days in most patients, restart using the initial titration schedule (do not resume the previous full dose). If stopped for ≤6 days, restart at a lower dose and climb back gradually based on prior dose and interacting medications.
adult.switch_ir_to_xr: When converting IR to XR, the XR starting dose typically matches the total daily IR dose, given once daily; monitor symptoms closely and adjust as needed, especially in patients on enzyme inducers.

sections.simple_explanation: Lamotrigine is a ‘slow ramp’ medication because the most dangerous side effect—severe rash—becomes more likely if you start too high or increase too quickly. That’s why dosing schedules look rigid. They’re not bureaucracy; they’re risk reduction.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Lamotrigine is often considered one of the more pregnancy-compatible mood stabilizer options, but pregnancy can lower lamotrigine blood levels and require dose adjustments. Breastfeeding exposure can be meaningful in some cases, so infants should be monitored.
sections.pregnancy: Lamotrigine crosses the placenta. During pregnancy, lamotrigine levels can drop significantly due to physiologic changes, which may require gradual dose adjustments and periodic blood level monitoring. After delivery, levels can rebound back toward baseline within weeks, so a plan to return to pre-pregnancy dosing helps reduce toxicity risk. In bipolar disorder, untreated illness also carries real risks, so decisions should be shared, individualized, and stability-focused rather than fear-based.
sections.lactation: Lamotrigine is present in breast milk, and infant serum levels can be measurable. Some infants exposed via breast milk have had drowsiness, poor feeding, poor weight gain, apnea, or rash. Many infants do well, but monitoring matters—especially in newborns and young infants who clear the drug more slowly.
sections.pediatrics: For psychiatric use, safety and efficacy for bipolar disorder in pediatric patients are not established in the same way as adult bipolar maintenance. Pediatric use is primarily in seizure disorders and requires careful titration due to rash risk.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults may be more sensitive to dizziness and fall risk. Use cautious titration, review other meds that increase falls, and consider additional cardiac risk screening when clinically appropriate.
sections.hepatic: If starting in moderate hepatic impairment, reduce initial and titration doses by about 25%. In severe hepatic impairment, reduction may be about 50%, especially if ascites is present. Immediate-release formulations can be easier to fine-tune when dose adjustments are needed.
sections.renal: No routine dose adjustment is typically required in mild to severe kidney impairment, but half-life can vary widely in significant renal disease. Titrate cautiously and monitor tolerability.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Rash surveillance (especially weeks 2–8): new rash, blistering, mucosal sores, facial swelling, eye irritation, fever, or feeling systemically ill needs prompt evaluation.
DRESS/HLH red flags: rash + fever + swollen lymph nodes + fatigue + lab abnormalities (CBC, LFTs) should trigger urgent assessment.
Mood tracking: depressive symptoms, mixed features, irritability, activation, and suicidality—especially early treatment and after dose changes.
Medication interaction monitoring: changes in valproate, enzyme-inducing meds, or estrogen-containing contraception can shift lamotrigine levels and side effects.
CBC if symptoms suggest blood dyscrasia: fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising, petechiae, recurrent infections.
Liver and renal function if clinically indicated or if symptoms suggest organ involvement (especially with hypersensitivity reactions).

ECG monitoring in higher-risk cardiac patients (eg, older adults with cardiac disease/risk factors, conduction disease, syncope without clear cause, or use of other sodium channel blockers) and repeat when target dose is reached if indicated.
Therapeutic drug monitoring when clinically useful (pregnancy, postpartum, major interaction changes, suspected toxicity or nonresponse).

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Lamotrigine comes in multiple oral forms, which helps with titration and tolerability. Formulation choice also matters if you need flexible dose adjustments.
items: Immediate-release tablets: multiple strengths (including scored tablets in many products)
Chewable/dispersible tablets: can be chewed, dispersed in water/diluted juice, or swallowed whole (useful for people who struggle with pills)
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT): dissolves on the tongue and can be swallowed with or without water
Extended-release tablets (XR): once-daily dosing; swallow whole (do not crush/chew/cut)
Oral suspension (brand availability may vary): useful for precise dosing in some settings

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Lamotrigine stabilizes overactive brain signaling by blocking voltage-sensitive sodium channels and reducing release of glutamate (an excitatory neurotransmitter). In bipolar disorder, that “signal smoothing” is thought to support mood stability over time, with a stronger effect on preventing depressive relapse than stopping acute mania.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Lamotrigine is a strong choice when bipolar depression is the main recurring problem and you need a maintenance plan that doesn’t rely on heavy sedation or weight-gain tradeoffs. It’s not a first-choice medication for acute mania because it titrates too slowly. In real-world care, it often pairs well with psychotherapy and lifestyle stabilization, and it may be combined with other mood stabilizers when mania risk is high—while keeping a close eye on interaction-driven dosing changes.

seo.title: Lamotrigine (Lamictal): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Rash Warning
seo.description: Lamotrigine (Lamictal) for bipolar disorder: what it treats, why titration is slow, dosing schedules with valproate/inducers, side effects, major interactions, and what to do about rash risk.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is lamotrigine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, lamotrigine is used for bipolar disorder—mainly as a maintenance medication to help prevent future mood episodes, especially bipolar depression. It’s not a PRN, and it’s not a strong medication for stopping acute mania.

faqs.q: How long does lamotrigine take to work?
faqs.a: Usually weeks. The dose has to be increased slowly to reduce the risk of dangerous rash, so you’re not “at a full dose” right away. Many people notice changes gradually during the titration phase or after reaching a steady maintenance dose.

faqs.q: Why is the lamotrigine titration so slow?
faqs.a: Because serious skin reactions (including SJS/TEN) are more likely when lamotrigine is started too high or increased too fast—especially with valproate. The schedule is designed to reduce that risk.

faqs.q: What should I do if I get a rash on lamotrigine?
faqs.a: Contact your prescriber immediately—especially if you’re in the first 2–8 weeks. If the rash comes with fever, mouth sores, blisters, eye irritation, facial swelling, or you feel very sick, treat it as urgent. Lamotrigine is usually stopped at the first sign of rash unless it’s clearly not medication-related.

faqs.q: Can lamotrigine help anxiety or insomnia?
faqs.a: Lamotrigine isn’t primarily an anxiety or sleep medication. Some people feel calmer as their mood stabilizes, but it’s not a fast anxiolytic and it’s not a sedative sleep aid. If anxiety or insomnia is the main issue, clinicians usually use other targeted treatments.
It’s usually considered more weight-neutral than many other bipolar medications. Some people gain or lose weight, but major weight gain is not the typical signature side effect.

faqs.q: What are the biggest drug interactions with lamotrigine?
faqs.a: Valproate raises lamotrigine levels (so dosing must be lower/slower). Enzyme inducers like carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and primidone lower levels (often requiring higher targets). Estrogen-containing birth control can lower levels and create swings across the pill cycle.

Don’t stop abruptly unless there’s a serious safety concern and a clinician tells you to (like a suspected severe rash). For routine discontinuation, tapering is recommended—often reducing about 50% per week over at least 2 weeks—while monitoring for mood relapse.

faqs.q: If I miss a week of lamotrigine, can I restart my old dose?
faqs.a: Usually no. If it’s been about a week or more, you typically restart at a low dose and re-titrate. Restarting at the old full dose can increase rash risk.

faqs.q: Is lamotrigine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Lamotrigine is commonly considered a more pregnancy-compatible mood stabilizer option than some alternatives, but pregnancy can lower lamotrigine levels and require monitoring and dose adjustments. It can pass into breast milk and infant levels can be measurable, so infants should be monitored for sedation, feeding problems, poor weight gain, apnea, or rash.

faqs.q: Does lamotrigine work for acute mania?
faqs.a: No—lamotrigine is not effective for treating acute mania or hypomania, and the slow titration makes it a poor tool for urgent manic symptoms. Clinicians typically use other medications for acute mania and use lamotrigine for longer-term mood stability.
